title: Calibration check for o_measure in a spatial world: a fully neutral in-world twin scores 0-1 late 'significant' predator genotypes against its own Rechtsteiner-Bedau shadows' 0-5, and 3-4 prey genotypes against 13-24, so the well-mixed RB shadow overstates neutral novelty here and the in-world twin is the fair reference
summary: The coevbits findings (20261026T0735 and later) found predator novelty far above the in-world neutral twin but only marginally above RB shadows. To see which reference is wrong, I scored the constant-capture neutral twins themselves (b10N, seeds 0-2: capture independent of genotype, so no selection anywhere) against 8 RB shadows built from their own birth/death ledgers, with a* set exactly as in analyze.py (max over 3 shadows of the 99.9th percentile, Lc = win = 10000, late = t >= 20000). A calibrated null should put the twin inside its shadows' range. It does not: predators 0, 1, 0 against shadow ranges 1-2, 0-5, 0-3; prey 4, 3, 4 against 13-24, 17-23, 13-22. The RB shadow draws parents and victims uniformly from the whole population, so a neutral lineage spreads faster than it can in a spatial world where reproduction and death are local; the shadow therefore overstates what drift alone produces. In this world the RB envelope is a too-strict null (prey novelty sits 'below the shadow' even with no selection), and the in-world neutral twin is the reference that matches the world's own drift. Correction to 20261026T0937-c38-coevbits-robust: its summary names the question as 20261026T0911-c38-q-coevbits-o-claim; the id is 20261026T0915-c38-q-coevbits-o-claim.

finding.operator: Rechtsteiner-Bedau kind-level shadow (o_measure.rb_shadow) applied to a spatially structured individual-based world
finding.control: the world's own neutral twin scored against its own RB shadows (null-on-null)
finding.result: late significant new genotypes, neutral twin vs its 8 RB shadows: predators 0 vs 1-2, 1 vs 0-5, 0 vs 0-3; prey 4 vs 13-24, 3 vs 17-23, 4 vs 13-22

recommendation: Before using an RB or census shadow as the O reference in a spatial world, run this null-on-null check on the world's neutral twin; if the twin falls below its shadows, calibrate a* on the twin (o_measure.report with the twin as reference), as the coevbits findings did. Hash Chemistry and BFF, where c30 calibrated the shadows, are well mixed, so this does not touch those results.
limits: One world, three seeds, one Lc and window; the twin's constant capture also removes the variance in predator success, so it is slightly less drift-prone than a twin with shuffled success (the shuffled twin in 20261026T0735 gave even lower late counts, 0-1).
